title: GA4 for Beginners
summary: Set up Google Analytics 4 the right way and read it with confidence: installation, events and key events, traffic sources, UTM tracking and the reports that show whether your marketing works.
outcomes:
Explain how GA4 measures users, sessions and events
Install GA4 on a website and confirm data is arriving
Mark the actions that matter as key events
Read traffic acquisition reports to see which channels bring results
Tag campaign links with UTM parameters so every source is tracked
Build a simple weekly report from GA4 data
description:
Google Analytics 4 (GA4) is the free tool most websites use to understand their visitors — but its interface confuses many beginners. This course cuts through it. You will learn how GA4 thinks about data, set it up correctly, track the actions that matter to your business, and read the handful of reports that answer real marketing questions.

Each lesson is short and practical, with a worked example, a checklist and an assignment you can do on your own site (or GA4's free demo account).
project: Set up (or audit) GA4 for a real website: confirm installation, choose and mark 2–4 key events, tag one campaign with UTM parameters, and write a one-page weekly report showing users, sessions by channel, key events by channel and one insight with a next step.

lessons.title: How GA4 thinks: users, sessions and events
lessons.intro: GA4 is built around one idea: everything a visitor does is an event. Once you understand users, sessions and events, every report in GA4 starts to make sense.
lessons.body:
The three building blocks

TermWhat it meansExample
UserA person (or more precisely a browser or device) visiting your sitePriya on her phone
SessionA group of interactions in one visitPriya's visit on Monday evening
EventA single actionViewing a page, scrolling, clicking a link, submitting a form

Everything is an event

Older analytics tools treated page views as the main unit. In GA4, a page view is just one type of event (page_view). A purchase, a sign-up and a video play are events too. This makes GA4 flexible: you can measure almost any action the same way.

Four kinds of events

  1. Automatically collected: GA4 records these with no setup, such as page_view, session_start and first_visit.
  2. Enhanced measurement: switch-on extras such as scrolls, outbound clicks, site search, video engagement and file downloads.
  3. Recommended events: names Google suggests for common actions, such as sign_up, generate_lead and purchase.
  4. Custom events: your own names for anything else.

Key events: the actions that matter

Most events are just activity. A few show real business results — a lead, a sign-up, a purchase, a booked call. In GA4 you mark those as key events so reports highlight them. (Older guides call these "conversions".)

Engagement, not bounce

GA4 counts a session as engaged if the visitor stayed a meaningful time, viewed more than one page, or triggered a key event. Engagement rate is the share of sessions that were engaged — a more useful number than old-style bounce rate.
lessons.example: An online course site wondered why its traffic reports looked healthy but sign-ups were flat. Once they understood that a sign-up was just another event — and marked sign_up as a key event — they could see which traffic sources produced sign-ups, not just visits.

lessons.title: Installing GA4 and checking it works
lessons.intro: A clean installation is the foundation of trustworthy data. This lesson walks through creating a GA4 property, adding the tag to your site and confirming that data is arriving.
lessons.body:
Step 1: Create an account and property

  1. Go to Google Analytics and sign in with a Google account the business controls (not a personal one that may leave).
  2. Create an account (usually your company) and a property (usually your website).
  3. Set the correct time zone and currency — reports and revenue depend on them.
  4. Add a web data stream for your website's URL. GA4 gives you a Measurement ID that starts with G-.

Step 2: Add the tag to your site

MethodBest for
Website builder or CMS setting (paste the G- ID)Shopify, Wix, Squarespace, many WordPress plugins
Google tag pasted into every page's <head>Simple custom websites
Google Tag ManagerSites where you will add more tags and events later

Use one method only. Installing GA4 twice is a common mistake that double-counts every page view.

Step 3: Check data is arriving

  • Open your site in another tab, then look at GA4's Realtime report — you should see yourself within a minute or two.
  • Use DebugView (with Tag Assistant) to watch individual events as they fire.

Step 4: Important settings

  • Enhanced measurement: leave it on unless an option causes problems.
  • Data retention: GA4 defaults to 2 months for detailed exploration data; standard properties can extend this to 14 months in Admin → Data settings. Do it on day one.
  • Internal traffic: define your office IP addresses as internal traffic and filter them out so your own visits don't inflate reports.
  • Consent: if you have visitors in regions that require cookie consent, make sure your consent banner and tags respect visitors' choices.
lessons.example: A small agency noticed its client's page views had doubled overnight with no change in sales. The developer had added the Google tag directly to the site while a plugin was already sending data to the same property. Removing one of them fixed the reports — and the Realtime check now became part of every launch.

lessons.title: Tracking what matters: events and key events
lessons.intro: Traffic is only useful if you can see which visits turn into results. Learn how to track sign-ups, leads and purchases as events and mark them as key events.
lessons.body:
Start with your business goals

Before touching settings, write down the 2–4 actions that matter most. For most sites these are:

  • Lead form submitted (generate_lead)
  • Account created or newsletter sign-up (sign_up)
  • Purchase completed (purchase)
  • Phone number or WhatsApp button clicked (a custom event such as click_to_call)

Three ways to get the event into GA4

  1. Already collected: some platforms (for example many e-commerce plugins) send purchase automatically. Check in DebugView.
  2. Create from an existing event: in Admin → Events → Create event, you can build a new event from a page view — for example generate_lead whenever someone views the /thank-you/ page.
  3. Send it from your site or Google Tag Manager: best for clicks and form submissions that don't lead to a separate page.

Mark it as a key event

Once the event appears in GA4, open Admin → Events (or Key events) and mark it as a key event. From then on it appears in key event columns across your reports. Marking is not retroactive, so do it early.

Give events a value

If a lead is worth roughly $40 to your business, send a value and currency with the event. GA4 can then show which channels produce the most value, not just the most events.

Keep it clean

  • Use Google's recommended event names where they fit.
  • Use lowercase names with underscores.
  • Don't mark everything as a key event — if everything is important, nothing is.
lessons.example: A dental clinic's booking form showed a thank-you page at /booking-confirmed/. They created a generate_lead event from page views of that URL and marked it as a key event. Within a week they could see that Google Business Profile visitors booked far more often than social media visitors.

modules.title: Module 2 · Reading GA4 and acting on it

lessons.title: Where visitors come from: traffic acquisition
lessons.intro: The traffic acquisition report answers the most common marketing question: which channels bring visitors who take action? Learn how to read it and avoid common misreadings.
lessons.body:
Find the report

Go to Reports → Acquisition → Traffic acquisition. Each row is a channel; the columns show sessions, engaged sessions, engagement rate, key events and revenue.

The default channel groups

ChannelWhat it usually means
Organic SearchUnpaid results from Google, Bing and other search engines
Paid SearchSearch ads
Organic Social / Paid SocialUnpaid posts / paid ads on social networks
EmailLinks in emails (needs UTM tags to be reliable)
ReferralLinks from other websites
DirectTyped URLs, bookmarks — and visits GA4 couldn't attribute

Read it like a marketer

  1. Sort by key events, not just sessions — the biggest channel isn't always the best.
  2. Compare engagement rate between channels to spot low-quality traffic.
  3. Calculate a simple key event rate per channel: key events ÷ sessions.
  4. Use the date picker to compare with the previous period.

Session vs first-user source

Traffic acquisition credits the source of each session. User acquisition credits the source that first brought each user. Use user acquisition to see what attracts new people; use traffic acquisition to see what brings visits that convert.

Beware large "Direct" numbers

A big Direct channel often hides untagged emails, messaging apps and links in PDFs. The fix is UTM tagging — the next lesson.
lessons.example: A software company's biggest channel by sessions was Organic Social, so they planned to post more. Sorting by key events showed Organic Search produced several times more demo requests from fewer sessions. They shifted effort into a few in-depth search articles instead.
lessons.checklist:
I can find the traffic acquisition report
I know what each default channel means
I sort channels by key events, not just sessions
I compare engagement and key event rates between channels
I know the difference between traffic and user acquisition
lessons.assignment: Open traffic acquisition for the last 28 days. Write down the top three channels by sessions and the top three by key events. What is different, and what would you do about it?

lessons.title: UTM parameters: tracking every campaign link
lessons.intro: UTM parameters are short tags added to links so GA4 knows exactly which email, post or ad sent each visitor. Learn the five parameters, a naming system and the mistakes to avoid.
lessons.body:
What a tagged link looks like

https://example.com/offer/?utm_source=newsletter&utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=spring-sale

The five UTM parameters

ParameterAnswersExample
utm_sourceWho sent the visitor?newsletter, facebook, linkedin
utm_mediumWhat type of channel?email, social, cpc, referral
utm_campaignWhich campaign?spring-sale, webinar-oct
utm_contentWhich version or link? (optional)video-ad, footer-link
utm_termWhich keyword? (optional, mostly paid search)crm-software

Use medium values GA4 understands

GA4 sorts traffic into channels partly from utm_medium. Use standard values such as email, social, cpc, paid_social, referral and affiliate. Made-up values like insta-story can end up in "Unassigned".

A simple naming system

  • Always lowercase (GA4 treats Email and email as different).
  • Use hyphens instead of spaces.
  • Keep a shared spreadsheet of every tagged link and its parameters.
  • Use a URL builder so links are typed the same way every time.

When not to use UTMs

Never add UTM tags to links within your own website — they restart the session and overwrite the real source. Google Ads usually doesn't need them either when auto-tagging is on.
lessons.example: A fitness brand sent the same offer by email, WhatsApp and an Instagram bio link. Before tagging, most of it showed as Direct. With UTMs (utm_source=whatsapp&utm_medium=social&utm_campaign=jan-challenge and so on), they found WhatsApp brought fewer visitors but the highest sign-up rate — and gave it a bigger role in the next launch.
lessons.checklist:
I know the five UTM parameters
I use standard medium values
All my UTM values are lowercase with hyphens
I keep a spreadsheet of tagged links
I never tag internal links on my own site
lessons.assignment: Create tagged links for your next email, one social post and one partner link. Record them in a simple spreadsheet with columns for URL, source, medium, campaign and content.

lessons.title: Your weekly GA4 report
lessons.intro: GA4 has dozens of reports, but you only need a few to run your marketing. Build a 15-minute weekly routine that turns data into one clear decision.
lessons.body:
The five reports to check each week

ReportWhereQuestion it answers
Reports snapshotReports → Reports snapshotAre users and key events up or down?
Traffic acquisitionAcquisition → Traffic acquisitionWhich channels bring results?
Pages and screensEngagement → Pages and screensWhich pages get attention?
Landing pageEngagement → Landing pageWhich entry pages convert?
Key eventsEngagement → Key eventsHow many results, and of which kind?

The 15-minute routine

  1. Set the date range to last 7 days and compare with the previous period.
  2. Note users, sessions, key events and key event rate.
  3. Check which channel moved the most, up or down.
  4. Find the landing page with the most sessions but a low key event rate — your biggest opportunity.
  5. Write one insight and one action for next week.

Explorations for deeper questions

When a standard report isn't enough, Explore lets you build custom tables and funnels. A funnel exploration (for example: landing page → sign-up page → sign-up complete) shows exactly where visitors drop out.

Share it simply

For a manager or client, a short summary beats a screenshot dump: three numbers, one chart, one insight, one next step. Looker Studio can turn GA4 data into a shareable dashboard when you're ready.
lessons.example: A course creator's weekly routine showed one blog post bringing a third of all landing-page sessions but almost no sign-ups. Adding a clear free-lesson offer halfway down the post turned it into the site's top sign-up source within a month.

I write one insight and one action every week
I know when to use an exploration

modules.title: Module 3 · Your GA4 setup and report

lessons.title: Final project: set up GA4 and write your first report
lessons.intro: Put everything into practice: set up or audit GA4 for a real website, track the actions that matter and write a one-page weekly report you could show a manager or client.
lessons.body:
What to deliver

  1. Setup check: property settings (time zone, currency), single installation confirmed in Realtime, data retention extended, internal traffic filtered.
  2. Key events: 2–4 key events, how each is tracked, and a test screenshot from DebugView.
  3. UTM plan: tagged links for one campaign across at least two channels, recorded in a spreadsheet.
  4. Weekly report: users, sessions by channel, key events by channel and key event rate — compared with the previous period.
  5. Insight and action: one finding and the change you would make next week.

How it is reviewed

A strong project is accurate (settings and events really work), focused (only the events that matter) and actionable (the report ends with a clear next step).
lessons.example: A local café audit: one installation confirmed, key events for click_to_call and table-booking form submissions, UTM-tagged links for an Instagram offer and a WhatsApp broadcast, and a weekly report showing Google Business Profile visitors booked most often — so the next action was adding fresh photos and posts to the profile.
